answers.text: A fixed three-line template — time, pallets, damage — pulled directly from the driver's message, not paraphrased. Anything the message doesn't cover still gets a line reading 'not stated'. Two runs match because there's no wording decision left, only slots to fill.

Split the week's entries into Needs follow-up and No action needed, one line per entry with time, customer, topic and outcome kept, and the count is just the size of the first list. A call that looks logged twice gets flagged rather than counted twice. None of that needs two people to have seen the same example.

The start time and duration don't support the stated finish date — 8am plus six hours is the same afternoon, the 22nd, not the 23rd. I'd confirm it against the crew's own sign-off log rather than assume the note is right.

96 to 118 invoices is roughly a 23% rise, not the 20% stated — that's the real error, not the on-time rate, which checks out at 9 of 118. The €58,000 balance split evenly is fine arithmetically, but it's never explained why it would hold flat against a 23% invoice rise. I'd check both against the regional ledgers directly.

Output 2 shows its working — 827 of 940 — so the 88% can be checked. Output 1 is just the answer with nothing behind it, so it can't be verified without rerunning the query. I'd still confirm 940 and 827 are the right totals before signing off.

Email 2, since the 1,200-to-1,650 volume increase is sourced from the PO log and can be checked. Email 1 makes the same kind of claim with no numbers attached. I'd pull the real figures from the PO log before Email 1 goes anywhere.

Line-item pricing: no. Total procurement spend: yes, aggregate only. The unsigned budget draft: no, not released. The vendor's own datasheet: yes, public. The employee's home address: no, personal data with no bearing here. Whether something's unreleased or identifies a person decides it each time.

The hourly rates and retainer cap I'd redact before pasting anything in. The non-disclosure clause names both companies, so that stays out too. The service scope on its own is low-risk enough to paste as it is.

The closing stock totals get cross-cast against the warehouse system myself, as the final step before the summary goes out — an actual comparison, not a read-through. That's what would catch a wrong figure or a line that doesn't exist in the real count. If something's off, it gets held and flagged.

A bad read at step 1 carries through everything after it, but step 4 is where it becomes irreversible, since the note sends automatically once the match is close enough. It should catch anything near the tolerance edge or missing from the original PO, and route a failed check to a person rather than leave it stopped with nobody told.
